## XI. The Battle of the Rams (1863)

Minister Adams troubled himself little about what he did not see of an enemy. His son, a nervous animal, made life a terror by seeing too much. Minister Adams played his hand as it came, and seldom credited his opponents with greater intelligence than his own. Earl Russell suited him—perhaps a certain personal sympathy united them; and indeed Henry Adams never saw Russell without being amused by his droll likeness to John Quincy Adams. Whether Russell were true or false mattered less, because in either case the American Legation could act only as though he were false. Russell was compelled, though slowly, to treat the American Minister as serious. He admitted nothing so unwillingly, for the nullity of the Washington Government was his *idée fixe*; but after the failure of his last effort for joint intervention in November 1862, he found himself on the defensive, with Mr. Adams taking daily a stronger tone.

Whatever the theory, the action of diplomacy had to be the same. If the escape of the *Alabama* might be ascribed to criminal negligence, no such concession could be made in regard to the ironclad rams the Lairds were building; for no one could be so simple as to believe that two armored ships-of-war could be built publicly, under the eyes of the Government, and go to sea without active and incessant collusion. The longer Earl Russell kept on his mask of assumed ignorance, the more violently in the end the Minister would have to tear it off.

As the spring of 1863 drew on, the vast field cleared itself for action. A campaign more beautiful—better suited for training the mind of a youth eager for training—has not often unrolled itself for study before a young man perched in so commanding a position. Very slowly, after two years of solitude, one began to feel the first faint flush of new and imperial life. One was twenty-five years old, and quite ready to assert it; some of one's friends were wearing stars on their collars. At moments one's breath came quick. The sense of unmeasured power came, like vertigo, for an instant, and passed, leaving the brain a little dazed, doubtful, shy. Little by little one began to feel that somewhere behind the chaos in Washington power was taking shape—massed and guided as it had not been before. Men had learned their business, at a cost that ruined, and perhaps too late. A private secretary knew better than most how much of the new power was to be swung in London, and almost exactly when; but the diplomatic campaign had to wait for the military campaign to lead.

Life never could know more than a single such climax. As the first great blows began to fall, one curled up in bed in the silence of night to listen with incredulous hope. As the huge masses struck, one after another with the precision of machinery, the world shivered. Such development of power was unknown. During the July days Londoners were stupid with unbelief. They were learning from the Yankees how to fight.

News of Vicksburg and Gettysburg reached London one Sunday afternoon, and it happened that Henry Adams was asked for that evening to a small reception at the house of Monckton Milnes. He went early to exchange a word of congratulation before the rooms should fill. Presently the gentlemen came in from their wine, and as luck would have it, Delane of the *Times* came first. When Milnes caught sight of his young American friend, with a whoop of triumph he rushed to throw both arms about his neck and kiss him on both cheeks. Men of later birth might conceive that such publicity embarrassed a private secretary who came from Boston and called himself shy; but that evening, for the first time in his life, he happened not to be thinking of himself. He was thinking of Delane, whose eye caught his at the moment of Milnes's embrace. Delane had never heard of young Adams, had no suspicion of his resentment at being ridiculed in the *Times*, and the capture of Vicksburg had not yet penetrated his thick cortex of fixed ideas. It needed a whole generation for the *Times* to reach Milnes's standpoint.

Vicksburg and Gettysburg cleared the board, and at the end of July 1863, Minister Adams was ready to deal with Earl Russell or Lord Palmerston or Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Delane—and by the necessity of the case was obliged to deal with all of them shortly.

In the Legation no great confidence was felt in stopping the rams. Whatever the reason, Russell seemed immovable. Little by little, Minister Adams lost hope. With loss of hope came the raising of tone, until at last, after stripping Russell of every rag of defence and excuse, he closed by leaving him loaded with connivance in the rebel armaments, and ended by the famous sentence: "It would be superfluous in me to point out to your lordship that this is war!"

What the Minister meant by this remark was his own affair; what the private secretary understood by it was a part of his education. Had his father ordered him to draft an explanatory paragraph, he would have continued thus: "It would be superfluous: 1st. Because Earl Russell not only knows it already, but has meant it from the start. 2nd. Because it is the only logical and necessary consequence of his unvarying action. 3rd. Because Mr. Adams is not pointing out to him that 'this is war,' but is pointing it out to the world, to complete the record." To his copying eye, as clerk, the words—though on the extreme verge of diplomatic propriety—merely stated a fact without novelty, fancy, or rhetoric. The war was Russell's war; Adams only accepted it.

Russell's reply, reaching the Legation on September 8, announced at last that "instructions have been issued which will prevent the departure of the two ironclad vessels from Liverpool." The members of the modest Legation in Portland Place accepted it as Grant had accepted the capitulation of Vicksburg. As Secretary Stanton had struck and crushed by superior weight the rebel left on the Mississippi, so Secretary Seward had struck and crushed the rebel right in England.

Though Minister Adams should stay in office till he were ninety, he would never fight another campaign of life and death like this. The private secretary felt respect for Russell and Palmerston because they represented traditional England—a policy respectable enough in itself, but one which, for four generations, every Adams had fought as the chief source of his political fortunes. Russell had followed this policy steadily, ably, even vigorously, and had brought it to the moment of execution. Then he had met wills stronger than his own, and, after persevering to the last possible instant, had been beaten. For once, the volunteer secretary was satisfied with his Government. The English campaign seemed to him as creditable to the State Department as the Vicksburg campaign to the War Department, and more decisive. He could never discover a mistake in it.

Yet the practical value of this education turned, in the end, on a question he could not settle. Again and again in after life he went back over the ground to see whether he could detect error on either side—and found none. All the more, then, was he disconcerted that Russell should indignantly deny, to his dying day, the axiom of Adams's whole contention: that from the first he had meant to break up the Union. Russell affirmed he meant nothing of the sort; that he had meant to do right; that he did not know what he meant. Driven from one defence after another, he pleaded at last, like Gladstone, that he had no defence—and then, to the total derision and despair of the lifelong effort for education, he proved it.

The evidence was, in the end, convincing. Russell had been feeble, timid, mistaken—but not dishonest. He had written to Palmerston on September 3, two days before Mr. Adams's "superfluous" letter, confessing that "the conduct of the gentlemen who have contracted for the two ironclads at Birkenhead is so very suspicious"—calling "the conduct" of the rebel agents *suspicious* when the whole question had never turned on the rams at all, but on the technical scope of the Foreign Enlistment Act. At the last moment he had reversed himself on grounds urged all along by the American Minister. For naivete that would have been unusual in an unpaid attaché, this sudden leap from his own ground to his opponent's, after two and a half years of dogged resistance, might have roused Palmerston to inhuman scorn. Instead, Palmerston met the appeal with wondering loyalty—and suggested buying the ships for the British Navy.

These letters, seen forty years later, upset from top to bottom the results of the private secretary's diplomatic education. They rendered worthless his whole painful experience. To reconstruct, past sixty, an education useful for any practical purpose is no practical problem, and Adams saw no use in attacking it as merely theoretical. He no longer much cared whether he understood human nature or not. He found in the *Life of Gladstone* a remark that gave him matter for curious thought: "I always hold that politicians are the men whom, as a rule, it is most difficult to comprehend"—and Gladstone added: "For my own part, I never have thus understood, or thought I understood, above one or two."

Earl Russell was certainly not one of the two. Henry Adams thought he also had understood one or two.
